Title: Report proposes new framework to prepare for future pandemics

Summary: 
Nearly five years after the onset of the COVID-19 pandemic, the Global Preparedness Monitoring Board (GPMB) has released a new report calling for a 'paradigm shift' in global pandemic preparedness. The report, launched at the World Health Summit in Berlin on October 14, 2025, warns that despite advances in science and technology, the world remains vulnerable due to persistent inequities, mistrust, and underinvestment in health systems. The GPMB, established in 2018 by the WHO and World Bank after the West Africa Ebola epidemic, emphasizes that the world is still not adequately prepared, with many countries failing to absorb the lessons of the pandemic. The report identifies three core actions for future readiness: 'Care', 'Measure', and 'Cooperate'. 'Care' calls for strengthening well-funded primary healthcare systems to detect outbreaks early, maintain essential services, protect healthcare workers, and build public trust. 'Measure' proposes a real-time pandemic risk monitoring system—described as an 'observatory'—that integrates epidemiological, economic, social, and environmental data using AI and other technologies to improve forecasting and decision-making. 'Cooperate' urges countries to ratify, implement, and finance the WHO Pandemic Agreement and its annex on Pathogen Access and Benefits Sharing, which aims to create equitable mechanisms for international collaboration. Joy Phumaphi, GPMB co-chair and former Botswana health minister, stated that pandemics are 'multidimensional shocks' requiring coordinated, multisectoral responses. Kolinda Grabar-Kitarović, GPMB co-chair and former Croatian president, stressed that resilient healthcare systems are essential for trust and effective response. The GPMB will work with the WHO and World Bank to ensure its recommendations are implemented at the 2026 United Nations High-Level Meeting on Pandemic Prevention, Preparedness, and Response.

Published date: October 14 2025, 19:51

URL: https://www.cidrap.umn.edu/public-health/report-proposes-new-framework-prepare-future-pandemics
Source: CIDRAP

Title: Africa: Four Years Later, Still No Clarity - WHO Report Highlights Gaps in Global Cooperation

Summary: 
The World Health Organization's (WHO) latest report on the origins of COVID-19 offers little new clarity and raises concerns about international cooperation and scientific transparency. The report, released by the WHO Scientific Advisory Group for the Origins of Novel Pathogens (SAGO), has been widely criticized for failing to break new ground. Much of the blame lies in the lack of transparency from China, which has not provided critical data requested by the investigation. Viscount Ridley, co-author of Viral: The Search for the Origin of Covid-19, said, 'The report adds almost nothing to what a few talented independent investigators found several years ago.' The search for COVID-19's origin is crucial for preventing the next pandemic, and scientists agree that future coronavirus outbreaks are not only possible but also likely. The WHO's Pandemic Agreement, adopted in May 2025, aims to strengthen preparedness for future outbreaks by improving cooperation and data sharing. However, some provisions remain under negotiation, and the lack of transparency and funding is hindering research vital to fighting COVID-19 and future respiratory diseases.

Published date: August 18 2025, 05:40

URL: https://allafrica.com/stories/202508180056.html
Source: allAfrica
Classification: Politics
Sentiment: negative
Reporting voice: Analytical
Continent: Africa

Title: The ongoing threat of new viral pathogens: An interview with Peter Daszak on a new coronavirus study

Summary: 
The World Socialist Web Site interview with Dr. Peter Daszak details a 2025 Nature.Health.Global study that found the swine acute diarrhea syndrome coronavirus (SADS‑CoV) is more diverse and dangerous than previously thought. The study analysed over 500 known viral sequences and added 186 new ones from Chinese bats, revealing at least two distinct coronavirus species. The horseshoe bat (Rhinolophus affinis) was confirmed as the main reservoir, with other species such as R. sinicus and R. thomasi also involved. Evidence points to Guangdong province as the origin of the first spillover into pigs, and the virus clusters locally, spreading mainly within regions rather than over long distances. In the lab, SADS‑CoV replicated efficiently in human lung and intestinal cells and killed newborn mice, signalling high spill‑over risk. Mapping bat habitats against pig and human populations identified southern China and northern Vietnam as pig‑infection hotspots, while the southern coast of China, Java and central Thailand were the greatest human‑risk areas. The virus has circulated in Chinese pigs since 2016, with near‑100 % mortality in piglets under five days old during the 2016, 2021 (Guangxi) and 2023 (Henan) outbreaks; 2022‑2023 surveys showed antibodies in nearly 60 % of herds across 29 provinces.

Daszak explains that the study’s findings are a "red flag" for spill‑over and that the political climate has severely hampered research. In May 2024 the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services barred EcoHealth Alliance and Daszak from federal funding for five years, a sanction usually reserved for proven fraud. By January 2025 Daszak was fired and EcoHealth dissolved, despite NIH approvals and no evidence of gain‑of‑function work. Daszak describes the hearings of the House Select Subcommittee on the Coronavirus Pandemic as "McCarthyite, anti‑science, anti‑democratic, anti‑China, and anti‑communist," and notes that the lab‑leak theory was treated as fact and EcoHealth was accused of wrongdoing.

Daszak says the new institute, Nature.Health.Global (NHG), was founded in April 2025 to continue pandemic‑prevention research while defending science from disinformation. NHG operates with private donors and state grants, and the SADS‑CoV paper was completed voluntarily by former EcoHealth staff who were laid off after the defunding. He stresses that the study is not about panic but about targeted surveillance: "If you can identify high‑risk regions, you can target your surveillance and prevention programs—spend less money, reduce more risk." The interview also critiques the Biden administration’s cuts to mRNA vaccine contracts and other research funding, arguing that defunding upstream science leaves the world vulnerable to future spill‑overs.

Daszak calls for a shift from reactive to preventive public‑health policy, emphasizing that "public health must come first" and that the U.S. retreat from science harms global pandemic preparedness. He warns that the political attacks on scientists have already damaged international collaboration, especially in China and Southeast Asia, and that without addressing the root causes—industrial farming, deforestation, wildlife trade—future pandemics are inevitable.

Key metrics from the study: 500+ known viral sequences, 186 new sequences, 150 unique bat‑derived sequences, 29 provinces with 60 % herd antibody prevalence, 100 % mortality in piglets during outbreaks, and local clustering of SADS‑CoV spread.

Published date: September 01 2025, 02:20

URL: https://www.wsws.org/en/articles/2025/09/01/dekw-s01.html
Source: World Socialist
Classification: Science
Sentiment: negative
Reporting voice: Narrative
Continent: Asia

</doc>

Title: 신종 코로나 바이러스 등장에 美긴장... "전염성 더 강해져"

Summary: 
A new coronavirus, HKU5-CoV-2, has been identified as having the potential to infect human cells with just one mutation, according to a recent study published in 'Nature Communications'. Although it is not currently a direct threat to humans, researchers warn that it is at an evolutionary stage close to being able to overcome host barriers. 'This virus can bind to the ACE2 receptor of bats with a single mutation, making it possible to infect human cells,' said researchers from the University of California. 'This could lead to a pandemic similar to the one caused by SARS-CoV-2.' The virus is classified as a Merbecovirus, the same family as the one that causes Middle East Respiratory Syndrome (MERS). Researchers emphasize the need for a strict monitoring system to prepare for the possibility of it becoming a zoonotic disease. Additionally, the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) and the World Health Organization (WHO) have issued a warning about the rapid spread of another variant, 'NB.1.8.1', also known as 'Nimbus'. This variant has been spreading rapidly in the UK, US, and Japan, and has been classified as a 'Variant Under Monitoring' by WHO. While it is believed to have some improved evasion capabilities, it does not appear to increase the severity of the disease. However, its rapid spread and transmission rate have raised concerns. Experts recommend that high-risk groups, such as the elderly and those with weakened immune systems, consider wearing masks and updating their vaccines. The CDC also expects the 2024-2025 seasonal COVID-19 vaccine to provide protection against this variant and recommends booster shots starting in the fall.

Published date: July 26 2025, 23:46
